People who had once been the best customers anyone could wish for now had no time to spare a thought for us. They said they were busy enough reading about revolutions and keeping pace with new ideas and the spirit of the times. If a fire needed air, a newspaper would do perfectly well to fan it. And as the government weakened, leather and iron must have grown stronger in equal measure: before long, not a single pair of bellows in Rotterdam needed a stitch or a stroke of the hammer. This situation was impossible to bear. I soon became as poor as a rat, and with a wife and children to support, my troubles eventually grew unbearable. I spent hours considering the most convenient way to end my life. Meanwhile, the people demanding payment left me little time to think. They practically surrounded my house from morning until night, until I began to rage and foam and pace like a caged tiger straining against its bars. Three men in particular tormented me past all endurance. They kept constant watch at my door and threatened legal action. In my heart I swore to take the bitterest revenge on these three if I ever had the good fortune to get my hands on them. I believe only the pleasure of looking forward to that moment kept me from immediately carrying out my plan to shoot myself in the head with a blunderbuss. Still, I thought it wiser to hide my anger and put them off with promises and pleasant words until some lucky chance gave me an opportunity for revenge.

“One day I managed to slip away from my creditors. Feeling even more miserable than usual, I wandered aimlessly for a long time through the least familiar streets, until I happened to bump into the corner of a bookseller’s stall. A chair for customers stood nearby. I dropped stubbornly into it and, scarcely knowing why, opened the first book within reach. It turned out to be a short pamphlet on Speculative Astronomy, written either by Professor Encke of Berlin or by a Frenchman with a somewhat similar name. I already knew a little about such subjects, and as I read I became increasingly absorbed in the book. In fact, I read it all the way through twice before I returned to an awareness of what was happening around me.

Four days after these strange events, a funeral procession left Canterville Chase at about eleven at night. Eight black horses pulled the hearse, each wearing an enormous tuft of swaying ostrich feathers on its head. A sumptuous purple cloth covered the lead coffin, with the Canterville coat of arms embroidered on it in gold. Servants carrying flaming torches walked beside the hearse and carriages, making the entire procession remarkably impressive. Lord Canterville, who had travelled from Wales especially for the funeral, was the principal mourner and rode in the first carriage with little Virginia. The United States Minister and his wife followed, then Washington and the three boys, while Mrs. Umney occupied the last carriage. Everyone generally agreed that, after being frightened by the ghost for over fifty years, she deserved to see the last of him. A deep grave had been prepared in a corner of the churchyard, directly beneath the old yew tree, and the Reverend Augustus Dampier conducted the service with great solemnity. After the ceremony, following an ancient Canterville family custom, the servants put out their torches. As the coffin was lowered, Virginia stepped forward and placed on it a large cross of white and pink almond blossoms. At that moment the moon emerged from behind a cloud, bathing the little churchyard in silent silver light, and a nightingale began singing in a distant grove. Remembering the ghost’s account of the Garden of Death, she felt tears blur her eyes and spoke scarcely a word on the journey home.

The following morning, before Lord Canterville left for London, Mr. Otis spoke with him about the jewels the ghost had given Virginia. They were truly magnificent, particularly a ruby necklace in an old Venetian setting, an exquisite example of sixteenth-century craftsmanship. Their immense value made Mr. Otis seriously question whether he could let his daughter accept them.

‘My lord,’ he said, ‘I understand that in this country the rules of mortmain, governing permanently held property, apply to ornaments as well as land. It seems perfectly clear that these jewels are, or ought to be, family heirlooms of yours. I must therefore ask you to take them to London and consider them simply part of your property, restored to you in unusual circumstances. As for my daughter, she is still only a child, and I am pleased to say she has so far shown little interest in accessories of this sort of idle luxury.

Few people had such a pure heart or combined such true humility with so firm a trust in their own honesty and the honesty of others. She had led a secluded life from birth. Her mother died when she was very young, but her father devoted himself to her education. He held many unusual ideas, and these shaped the way he taught her. She knew the heroes of Greece and Rome well, along with English heroes who had lived centuries earlier, yet she knew almost nothing about the events of her own day. She had read few writers from the past fifty years or more, though apart from this gap she had read very widely. So, although she seemed to understand less about life and society than he did, her knowledge went deeper and rested on stronger foundations. Even if her beauty and kindness had failed to fascinate him, her intelligence would always have held his mind captive. He looked to her for guidance. He adored her so much that he took pleasure in strengthening his own sense of being inferior to her, a feeling she sometimes inspired.

His mother died when he was nineteen. He left college after her death and, withdrawing for a time from his old friends, went to live near his Diana. Her gentle voice and still more precious caresses gave him all his comfort. This brief separation from his companions gave him the courage to claim his independence. He felt that, however much they might ridicule his planned marriage, they would not dare to do so once he was married. He therefore asked his guardian’s permission, which he obtained with some difficulty, and the permission of his beloved’s father, who agreed more readily. Without telling anyone else what he intended, he became Diana’s husband by the time he reached his twentieth birthday.

He loved her passionately, and her tenderness had such power over him that he could think of nothing but her. He invited some college friends to visit, but their shallow behaviour disgusted him. Diana had lifted the veil that had kept him a boy. Now he was a man, and he wondered how he could ever have shared his fellow students’ empty phrases and ideas, or feared their disapproval even for a moment. He gave up his old friendships because those friends were truly unworthy of him, rather than from any tendency to change his affections.
